samples.summary: `list`/`revoke` default to an UNSCOPED (owner-level) scope when the argument is omitted — a fail-open default on the only creator-ownership check
samples.evidence: `async list(workspaceId, scope: KeyScope = {})` (api-key.service.ts:55) and `async revoke(id, workspaceId, scope: KeyScope = {})` (api-key.service.ts:92) treat a missing scope as "every key in the workspace". The whole creator boundary introduced by this change lives in a default parameter, so any call site that forgets the third argument silently gets workspace-wide listing/revocation with no compile-time error. I enumerated today's callers with `Grep 'apiKeyService\.'` over packages/backend/src: only ApiKeyController.list:65 and .revoke:77 call them, and both pass `keyScope(...)`, so there is no live bypass — but the service's own spec already exercises the unscoped form (`service.revoke('k1','ws-1')`, api-key.service.spec.ts:127), which is exactly the shape a future caller would copy. Making `scope` a required parameter (`KeyScope` with an explicit `{}` for owners) makes the owner case a deliberate, greppable decision instead of an omission. Attack requires a future/overlooked caller, hence minor.

samples.summary: Any member can now mint unlimited, never-expiring `read+write` bearer credentials; no per-user cap, no default expiry, no owner notification
samples.evidence: `create` is now gated only on `assertMember` (api-key.controller.ts:47) while `ApiKeyService.create` defaults to `scopes: ['read','write']` and `expiresAt: expiresAt ?? null` (api-key.service.ts:42-43), i.e. a permanent credential. The controller carries no `@Throttle`; only the global 120/min ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:97-130) applies, so a member (or malware in a member's browser session, since these routes accept the session cookie) can mint an unbounded number of long-lived tokens that outlive the browser session and any future session-revocation/MFA. Removal does kill them (`WorkspaceService.removeMember` bulk-revokes in the same transaction, workspace.service.ts:115-124) and `WorkspaceScopeGuard` re-checks membership live, so the blast radius is bounded to the member's own authority — this is the accepted design, but a default expiry and a per-user key cap would be cheap hardening now that minting is open to every member. I did not find a key-count limit anywhere (grepped the api-key module and workspace service).

samples.summary: Revoked-row read-back is keyed on `id` alone, unscoped by workspace or creator — safe only because the preceding count check is right
samples.evidence: After the scoped `updateMany`, the returned row is fetched with `findUnique({ where: { id } })` (api-key.service.ts:108-118), dropping both `workspaceId` and `createdBy` from the predicate. It is correct today: `result.count === 0` throws first (line 104-106), so reaching the read implies the id matched the scoped filter. But the safety is entirely carried by a separate statement; if the count branch is ever relaxed or reordered, this line hands a caller another workspace's / another member's key metadata (`name`, `prefix`, `scopes`, `createdBy`). Repeating the same `where` in the read-back costs nothing and keeps the scoping local.
